description: We are Digital Heroes, a team participating in Irbid. We aim to explore Earth system trends using NASA data and turn our findings into clear, engaging visual stories. We welcome curious teammates interested in data analysis, coding, Earth science, and design. Together, we hope to build a useful project and learn from each other!
summary:
Is Irbid hotter than the countryside around it? Earth Trend Detective lets you explore that question on an interactive map. We used NASA Terra MODIS data to compare summer land surface temperatures in Irbid, Jordan, and its surroundings from 2001 to 2024. You can switch between day and night, see how temperatures changed over time, and check whether the evidence points to a clear trend.

The app also takes you to a pilot field in Huwwarah, where you can replay a wheat season in 3D, from planting to harvest. You can explore how the crop responds to weather and compare a rainfed season with one that uses supplemental irrigation. We label satellite observations and simulations separately so farmers and students can see which results come from measurements and which come from the model.
details:
Earth Trend Detective is an interactive web app for exploring temperature trends and farming scenarios in Jordan. It brings together three views that let users go from a country-scale map to a single field in Huwwarah.

In the Irbid Case, we used NASA Terra MODIS observations to compare summer land surface temperatures in the city and its surroundings from 2001 to 2024. Users can switch between daytime and nighttime observations and inspect the evidence behind each result. During the day, Irbid’s surface was about 2.8°C cooler than the surrounding area on average across the 24 summers studied. The country view uses ERA5-Land to show trends in summer air temperature for the countries included in the pilot dataset.

At the Huwwarah pilot field, users can examine satellite-based vegetation and rainfall estimates and replay a modeled wheat season in 3D. They can choose a date, follow the crop from growth to harvest, and compare rainfed and supplemental irrigation scenarios. NASA GPM IMERG adds half-hourly precipitation estimates where data are available. The interface distinguishes satellite observations, gridded estimates, and simulations so users can tell what supports each result.

We built the app with TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, and Three.js. The crop replay uses AquaCrop simulation outputs, and Google Earth Engine was used for geospatial data processing. Our goal is to make local questions about heat, crops, and water easier to investigate for farmers, students, and other users who want to explore the evidence for themselves.
